transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-28
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marta Gomez (BrightPath Head of ML), Ethan Park (BrightPath Infra), Samir Patel (BrightPath Product), Lina Zhao (BrightPath Data Scientist)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console sandbox focusing on INT8 vs FP8 quantization profiles and tradeoffs between latency, throughput, cost, and accuracy.
- Ran a few live micro-benchmarks with their sample prompts; discussed fallback rules, prefix KV caching, and rollback strategies.
- Action items: sandbox creds, perf logs from Priya, prompt set from BrightPath.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): All right, good afternoon everyone. Thanks for carving time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya, our systems engineer who does the deep in the quant profiles. How are you all?
[00:12] Marta (Head of ML): Hey Jordan, good thanks. Excited to see the sandbox. We had a quick internal chat about what success looks like — basically latency under 300ms p50 for short chat queries, cost below our current hosted baseline, and no visible quality regressions on the medical triage prompts.
[00:28] Jordan: Great, that's helpful. Priya, quick intro?
[00:31] Priya (SE): Yeah hi everyone. I'm Priya. I run model onboarding and the Optimize profiles. Today we'll step through the console, show the INT8 and FP8 profiles we tested, demo the tradeoff matrix and live compare a few prompts. Fair warning the transcription may garble some kernel names, but I'll say them out loud.
[00:47] Ethan (Infra): Quick question — are we testing on your hosted infra or on the dedicated sandbox you provisioned? We gave you the sample dataset earlier.
[00:55] Priya: This is the Redwood sandbox running in our shared eval cluster, it's not your VPC; we can repro on Dedicated or Private later. For the demo the HW is A100-ish equivalent with mixed precision support.
[01:06] Samir (Product): And the cost numbers you show will be rough estimates, right? We care about per-1k-token costs and also tokenized prompt lengths for triage.
[01:14] Jordan: Correct, the cost worksheet we'll send has per-token estimates and estimated monthly run-rate based on your traffic shape.

[01:22] [00:60] Priya: Okay jumping into the console — here's the Optimize view. You'll see two active profiles for the model we uploaded: bp-med-001-int8 and bp-med-001-fp8. The console auto-generated a sensitivity score for each prompt bucket; red means higher risk.
[01:40] Marta: That sensitivity scoring — is that per prompt or per intent?
[01:44] Priya: It's per prompt cluster, derived from a small eval set you provided plus synthetic paraphrases. We run a fidelity check comparing logits on a float baseline and then aggregate on a pass/fail. The scoring can be tuned; you can link it to your golden set in the sandbox.

[01:58] [02:00] Jordan: We prepared three demo prompts — a short triage question, a medium clinical summary, and a longer policy extraction. We'll run all three across INT8, FP8, and the float baseline.
[02:12] Priya: Running short triage now — one tokenized prompt, about 24 tokens. Latency's ~210ms p50 on FP8, 160ms on INT8; cost shows INT8 about 22% cheaper per token in this sandbox.
[02:31] Lina (Data Scientist): Wait — that's interesting, INT8 is faster here? I usually expect FP8 to be faster because of the SIMD path.
[02:38] Priya: Good call — it's because the runtime selected a different kernel for this sequence length; INT8 benefited from a fused matmul kernel with better mem locality. With longer context FP8 can win. There's also KV cache interplay — for short two-turn chats the cache warmup overhead matters.
[02:52] Ethan: Any effect from cosine quantization? We saw in other vendors that per-channel quant leads to variance.
[02:58] Priya: We support symmetric and asymmetric per-channel quant; in this profile we used per-channel symmetric with a small bias-correction pass. That reduced outliers on certain numeric tokens.

[03:12] [03:15] Jordan: Ok run the medium one please.
[03:18] Priya: Medium clinical summary — about 180 tokens. FP8 p50 ~420ms, INT8 p50 ~520ms. So here FP8 is faster, but FP8 shows a slight drop in Rouge-L on one of the gold summaries — about 1.8 points.
[03:35] Marta: 1.8 Rouge-L — that might be perceptible. Can you show the generation side-by-side?
[03:39] Priya: Sure. (screen) Baseline float: "Recommend in-person evaluation and vitals capture. Possible differential includes..." FP8: "Recommend in person evaluation and vitals monitoring..." INT8: "Suggest evaluate in person and check vitals, possible..." The INT8 version sometimes swaps phrasing, and there are small abbreviations.
[03:58] Samir: That swap could change product behavior if we automate triage. Our OLQ threshold is pretty strict for safety-critical phrasing.
[04:06] Priya: Understood. That's where the sensitivity buckets come in — you can map higher-risk intents to stricter rollback rules or force float baseline for that bucket.

[04:16] [04:30] Lina: If we force float for some intents, does that create a capacity isolation concern?
[04:22] Jordan: Yes it will. If many requests require float we can either increase Dedicated capacity or set an autoscale burst that lands on a higher-cost pool. We'll include cost scenarios in the worksheet.

[04:34] [04:45] Ethan: How deterministic are the regressions? If we see a 1.8 Rouge-L drop on one prompt, is it consistent across seeds?
04:49 Priya: Most of these are reproducible; we use a fixed sampling config for the eval (top-p/top-k/temperature). But there are nondeterministic sources at the kernel level if you're using certain fused ops — we can lock deterministic kernels for the pilot. That may increase latency slightly.

[05:05] [05:15] Jordan: Priya, can you show the rollback playbook?
[05:18] Priya: Yeah — the rollout plan in the console: starting with 5% traffic on INT8, monitor fidelity score, then 25%, 50%, 100% if pass thresholds. Automatic fallback to FP8 or float if fidelity < threshold OR if error rates spike. You can set stricter thresholds per intent.
[05:33] Marta: If fallback triggers, do you preserve the original request context for re-run? We'd prefer single-call fallback without double-billing the customer.
[05:40] Priya: Current flow for hosted uses an internal retry that doesn't double-charge tokens to you for the experiment window — it re-executes on the fallback path but we attribute cost to the fallback pool; we can annotate billing. For Private deployments billing behavior depends on your contract but logs show both attempts.

[05:55] [06:00] Ethan: About the cache — we saw some variance earlier. How do you handle prefix caching across quant profiles?
[06:03] Priya: KV cache is stored in a format that's compatible across profiles if dimensionality matches. We quantize weights not the activations; the cache store is separate. However certain extreme quant schemes change the key layout and require cache invalidation. The console warns you when a profile will invalidate cache.

[06:20] [06:30] Priya: Now I'll kick off a 100-query micro-benchmark across all profiles to show distribution. This will take a few minutes — you'll see p50/p95 and token-level cost breakdown.
[06:40] Samir: While that's running can you describe the quality monitoring? We need alerts when fidelity degrades over time.
[06:46] Priya: We have a drift monitor that runs on a supplied golden set and also on live samples (scrubbed). It computes fingerprint diffs and flags regressions by absolute and relative deltas. Alerts can be Slack/PagerDuty/email. You can also tie an auto-rollback if a threshold is hit.

[06:58] [07:05] (benchmark log noise in background)
[07:12] Priya: Okay first run finished. Short prompt stats: INT8 p50 155ms, p95 310ms, FP8 p50 208ms, p95 360ms, float baseline p50 420ms. Accuracy pass rate on the short triage pack: INT8 98%, FP8 99.2%.
[07:40] Marta: Those numbers are promising. On the medium set?
[07:44] Priya: Medium: FP8 pass rate 92%, INT8 89%, float 94%. So you see a gap.
[07:52] Lina: Could early stopping or tokenization differences cause that?
[07:55] Priya: Possibly. We normalize tokenization across profiles in the eval harness, but generation heuristics can interact with logits scaling. We also ran a micro calibration step for INT8 to reduce bias, but that sometimes decreases expressivity.

[08:10] [08:20] Jordan: A few enterprise questions that often come up — SOC2, SSO, KMS. Marta mentioned compliance: what's needed for a Private deploy?
[08:27] Marta: Yeah sorry to jump in — for PHI-sensitive prompts we'd likely need a Private VPC option, KMS, and audit trails. Also retention controls.
[08:35] Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, full audit logs, and can be deployed in your VPC or on-prem. We'll scope that in the pilot phase; typically security review + PoC within 4–8 weeks.
[08:46] Ethan: Network egress — if we run Dedicated, can we pin region for residency?
[08:50] Priya: Yes, routing policies allow region pinning and site affinity. For Dedicated we can reserve capacity in the region of your choice.

[08:58] [09:10] Samir: Back to costs — can you show the per-month estimate if we run 50 million tokens a month with 60% short triage, 30% medium, 10% long extraction and 30% fallback to float?
[09:22] Jordan: We'll calculate that. The worksheet factors in p50 token usage, fallback distribution, and reserved capacity seats. We'll send two scenarios: conservative and optimistic.

[09:30] [09:40] Priya: One more thing — profile mixing. You can use a hybrid policy: prefer INT8 unless sensitivity > X, then FP8, else float. That often yields the best cost/loss balance. The console UI shows heatmaps for expected cost savings per-intent.
[09:56] Marta: Can we lock a per-prompt rule? For instance anything with "chest pain" goes float baseline always.
[10:01] Priya: Absolutely, per-intent mapping or regex-based rules are supported. You can also tag prompts to group them.

[10:10] [10:20] (Benchmark continues, small pause)
[10:28] Priya: Final aggregate: estimated token savings compared to float: INT8 ~38% cost reduction, FP8 ~23% reduction in this cluster. But FP8 reduces latency on medium/long sequences in general.
[10:45] Lina: That 38% seems high. Why that much?
[10:48] Priya: In our sandbox the fused INT8 kernel improved throughput significantly for small contexts; your real numbers may vary but trends are similar. We'll provide the raw logs so you can verify.

[11:00] [11:10] Ethan: Regarding rollback velocity — if a new int8 profile shows issues, how fast can we revert globally?
[11:15] Priya: It's an immediate routing change in the control plane — within seconds for hosted; Dedicated may be subject to drain windows depending on your autoscale settings. We have a canary window you can tune to 0 if you want immediate fallback.

[11:27] [11:40] Samir: Any gotchas with tokenizer differences across models? If we swap to a smaller LLM, do profiles transfer?
[11:45] Priya: Profiles are model-specific. We provide a profile export/import tool but recommend re-profiling when switching models or major sequence-length distributions. Some quant profiles port better if the architecture is identical.

[11:55] [12:05] Jordan: Let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[12:07] Marta: Quick clarification — the drift alerting uses both absolute metric thresholds and relative historical baselines?
[12:12] Priya: Yes both. You can configure alert sensitivity in the console.
[12:15] Jordan: Recap items: 1) Jordan sends sandbox access and the cost worksheet. 2) Priya shares raw micro-benchmark logs and the seed config used for eval. 3) Marta provides the labeled prompt set and defines safety-critical intents. 4) We schedule a pilot kickoff after you review the numbers.
[12:35] Jordan: Anything else?
[12:38] Marta: Please note we may require a short security questionnaire for Private deployment. We'll send that to Jordan.
[12:44] Jordan: Got it. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed pilot timeline.
[12:49] (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: speaker labels sometimes generic; slight OCR/transcription noise around kernel names and acronyms (A100-esque, K V cache typed as K V).
